notes: Section 151 financial assistance challenge to liquidation proofs; agreed market rent excess and outcome are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Section 151 financial assistance and liquidation proofs
key_facts: Mrs Dyment acquired the Bishops' shares in a residential care company and gave up her interest in The Mount while the Bishops granted a 21-year lease at £66,000 per annum.
The company paid only £3,350 per month rent; the Bishops obtained summary judgment for £140,017.63 and controlled the liquidation through that proof.
It was agreed the initial market rent was £37,000 and the lease reduced the company's net assets to a material extent.
Mrs Dyment sought to expunge the proofs on the basis that the lease contravened section 151 and was void.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim under the Insolvency Act and Rules challenging proofs of debt in a creditors' voluntary liquidation.
enrichment.outcome: Section 151 point failed; the lease was not financial assistance for the share acquisition and remaining discretionary issues were not decided.
enrichment.ratio: Where a company enters an onerous lease to obtain premises needed to continue trading after a buy-out, and the excessive rent reflects the freeholders' negotiating power rather than the purpose of acquiring shares, section 151 is not infringed even though the transaction is connected with the share transfer.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Dyment had locus standi to challenge proofs under Insolvency Rules 4.83 and 4.85
Whether the lease constituted financial assistance under section 151(1) or (2)
Whether breach of section 151 rendered the lease void and unenforceable
Whether the liquidator was bound by the rent judgment when admitting the proofs

notes: Mandatory condemnation under Food Safety Act section 9 is clearly resolved; declaratory relief granted.

enrichment.short_title: Mandatory condemnation of non-compliant food under section 9
key_facts: An authorised officer detained 32 boxes of beef forequarters at Kelman Kosher Products for lack of required health marking on packaging.
District Judge Marshall upheld non-compliance but exercised a discretion not to condemn the meat because labelling defects did not affect fitness for consumption.
The Food Standards Agency sought declaratory relief after the judge refused to state a case.
The meat had already been released, sold and consumed before the hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review seeking declaratory relief on the interpretation of section 9 Food Safety Act 1990.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration granted that a justice of the peace must condemn food failing food safety requirements and has no discretion to release it.
enrichment.ratio: Once a justice of the peace is satisfied on appropriate evidence that detained food fails to comply with food safety requirements, section 9(6) requires mandatory condemnation; subsection (7)'s reference to refusing to condemn means only that condemnation is not established, not that a discretion exists.
legal_issues: Whether a justice exercising powers under section 9 acts as a court amenable to case stated procedure
Whether section 9(6) confers a discretion not to condemn non-compliant food
Proper interpretation of section 9(7) compensation provisions
Whether declaratory relief was appropriate where the food had already been consumed

notes: Post-appeal defamation damages assessment; statutory cap and restructuring effect clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Corporate libel damages capped after insolvency letters
key_facts: The Court of Appeal had entered summary judgment for Downtex on libel claims over two letters circulated to about twenty suppliers alleging insolvency and director misconduct.
Mr Flatley circulated the letters in June 2002 after a deteriorating commercial relationship following a business purchase.
Downtex later restructured in December 2003, hiving its business into Carrwood Ltd and ceasing to trade under the name referred to in the libel.
Damages were assessed without a jury and without live defendant representation at the hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Assessment of libel and contractual damages following Court of Appeal summary judgment under the Defamation Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Libel damages assessed at the £10,000 section 8 cap; breach of contract damages assessed at £10 nominal.
enrichment.ratio: A serious corporate libel alleging trading while insolvent to existing suppliers warrants substantial general damages, but where summary relief under section 8 applies the award is capped at £10,000 and later corporate restructuring reduces the vindication element though not damage already suffered.
legal_issues: Proper approach to assessing damages under section 8 where the statutory cap applies
Whether a corporation may recover injury to feelings
Effect of subsequent corporate restructuring on libel damages
Avoidance of double counting between libel and contractual claims

notes: Complex Tomlin Order and Newbuild scheme dispute; all claims dismissed with detailed procedural history.

enrichment.short_title: Tomlin Order enforcement and Newbuild scheme dispute
key_facts: Zurich removed Carabos from its Newbuild indemnity scheme after Mr Goodway refused to reimburse about £60,000 for drainage works at two Wootton properties.
The parties compromised consolidated county court proceedings in a Tomlin Order requiring £80,000 in tranches, independent surveys and escrow security for two Ryde houses.
Implementation stalled amid disputes over surveyor appointment, scope of surveys and remedial works recommended in Mr Needham's report.
Mr Goodway obtained alternative Premier Guarantee cover in February 2003 and did not intend to complete the Tomlin procedure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court applications to enforce a Tomlin Order and cross-claims to set it aside or recover misrepresentation damages.
enrichment.outcome: Zurich's mandatory enforcement application and Goodway and Carabos's cross-claims dismissed; parties had mutually failed to cooperate.
enrichment.ratio: A Tomlin Order implementing an insurer/builder settlement carries implied duties of mutual cooperation and reasonable expedition; where both sides delay, obstruct and evince an intention not to be bound, neither mandatory enforcement nor rescission for misrepresentation will succeed.
legal_issues: Whether Zurich was entitled to an order requiring remedial works following the independent survey
Whether Zurich's delays breached implied terms of the Tomlin Order
Whether non-disclosure of costings induced an unduly unfavourable settlement
When Zurich could recover the outstanding £60,000 tranche

notes: Drainage easement change-of-use appeal; two-stage test and expert flow evidence clearly analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Drainage easement after bakery replaced by houses
key_facts: A bakery on land sold in 1982 enjoyed an implied drainage easement through a pipe under neighbouring Whyte Cottage into the public sewer.
McAdams demolished the bakery and built two four-bedroom houses, intending to use the same pipe.
The Robinsons blocked the pipe because of sewage backflow concerns; McAdams built a new drain at a cost of £6,633.26.
Expert evidence indicated residential use would generate substantially greater flow than the bakery.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court claim for the cost of a replacement drainage system after interference with an easement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the easement could not lawfully be used for the redeveloped residential houses.
enrichment.ratio: An implied drainage easement granted on a sale under Wheeldon v Burrows is lost or suspended where redevelopment represents a radical change in the character of the dominant land and results in a substantial increase in the burden on the servient land, assessed by comparing likely flows rather than pipe capacity alone.
legal_issues: Whether blocking the pipe before the houses were built defeated the claim
Whether sewage backflow from a defective public sewer justified blocking the pipe
Whether replacement of a bakery by two houses was a radical change of character
Whether increased drainage flow imposed a substantial additional burden

enrichment.short_title: Licence recall credit on consecutive burglary sentence
key_facts: The appellant pleaded guilty to a dwelling-house burglary committed on 7 August 2002 while on licence from an earlier four-year-nine-month sentence.
He was sentenced to return to prison for the full unexpired balance of the earlier sentence plus four years consecutive for the new offence.
Sixty of 174 days in custody before sentencing arose from administrative licence revocation rather than remand on the new offence.
A post-sentencing psychological report did not justify reducing the four-year term.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission following refusal of leave to appeal against sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; the section 116 return period was reduced by 90 days to reflect 60 days served following licence revocation.
enrichment.ratio: Time spent in custody following administrative recall of licence should ordinarily be recognised when fixing the period of return to custody under section 116, grossed up for a long-term prisoner, unless it will in any event be credited against the new sentence.
legal_issues: Whether fresh psychological evidence warranted reducing the four-year sentence
Whether 60 days served after licence revocation should reduce the section 116 term
Application of section 67 Criminal Justice Act 1967 to recall time
Effect of R v Sharkey and R v Stocker on consecutive recall sentences

R v Stocker [2003] 2 Cr App R(S) 54

notes: University visitor judicial review on narrow Page grounds; permission refused with clear reasoning.

enrichment.short_title: Bradford University visitor review of PhD grievance refused
key_facts: Mr Deman's PhD thesis was deemed insufficient for a doctorate and he was offered an MPhil after a long academic history at Bradford University.
He appealed to the Grievance Committee on bias grounds, but the Pro-Vice-Chancellor found a prima facie case only on prejudice or bias and not on his other complaints.
The Lord Chancellor as visitor reviewed the committee decision and rejected intervention.
Mr Deman had previously pursued but lost a separate racial discrimination claim in the ordinary courts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission for judicial review of the visitor's decision on a university grievance appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; the visitor acted within jurisdiction and an alternative statutory remedy barred visitor review.
enrichment.ratio: Courts will not review a university visitor for mere error of law; intervention requires jurisdictional error, abuse of power or breach of natural justice, and a visitor may reject a petition where an alternative statutory remedy exists even if unused on the merits.
legal_issues: Whether the visitor erred in his treatment of racial bias allegations
Whether the Grievance Committee could consider grounds beyond those referred by the Pro-Vice-Chancellor
Scope of judicial review of visitor decisions after R v Hull University Visitor ex parte Page
Whether discrimination allegations altered the visitor jurisdiction test
linked_authorities: R v Hull University Visitor, ex parte Page [1993] AC 682

confidence.notes: Permission refusal and Page principles are clearly applied. Underlying academic merits were not decided.

enrichment.short_title: Legal privilege on copyright damages inquiry
key_facts: HHJ Weeks held LGH infringed USP's copyright and confidentiality in a Collections Account Agreement used in bidding for a Powerhouse warranty scheme.
Damages inquiry turned on whether privileged Manx legal advice forwarded to Powerhouse could be used to prove an earlier February 2000 infringement.
Defendants redacted disclosed correspondence with Powerhouse and sought to strike witness statement passages referring to Cains legal advice.
A separate Apollo transaction royalty claim also raised privilege over drafts sent to solicitors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications on legal professional privilege, witness statement redaction and disclosure for a copyright damages inquiry.
enrichment.outcome: Level 1 and 2 references not privileged; Level 3 advice content generally protected subject to specified witness-statement excisions; defendants ordered to serve a further list of documents.
enrichment.ratio: Summaries or extracts of legal advice communicated to a third party under confidentiality remain capable of legal advice privilege unless waived; waiver to Powerhouse under a strict confidentiality agreement was limited and did not permit competitors to deploy the substance of the advice.
legal_issues: Whether paraphrases of legal advice sent to Powerhouse were privileged
Whether privilege was waived by partial deployment in earlier proceedings
Whether witness evidence of advice obtained in breach of confidence should be excluded
Whether copies of the CAA sent to solicitors for advice attracted privilege

notes: Three Rivers privilege appeal on Bingham Inquiry advice; narrow legal-advice meaning clearly adopted.

enrichment.short_title: Three Rivers legal advice privilege at Bingham Inquiry
key_facts: Following BCCI's collapse, the Bank of England retained Freshfields to assist its Bingham Inquiry Unit in preparing evidence and submissions.
In Three Rivers (No 5) the Court of Appeal held third-party documents prepared for the inquiry were not privileged because they were not solicitor-client communications.
The liquidators then challenged privilege in communications passing directly between Freshfields and the BIU.
The dominant purpose of Freshfields' work was presentation of evidence to minimise criticism rather than advice on legal rights and obligations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a declaration limiting legal advice privilege in disclosure proceedings arising from BCCI liquidation litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; only communications seeking or evidencing advice on the Bank's legal rights and obligations were privileged.
enrichment.ratio: Legal advice privilege covers advice on legal rights and liabilities, not general assistance on presenting evidence to a non-statutory inquiry to protect reputation; presentation advice to the Bingham Inquiry did not attract privilege even where some legal-rights advice may also have been given.
legal_issues: Whether Three Rivers (No 5) had already decided privilege in BIU-Freshfields communications
Meaning of 'legal advice' for legal advice privilege
Whether inquiry presentation assistance is privileged
Whether concern to protect regulatory reputation equates to legal rights and obligations

notes: Extradition in absentia with co-operator safety fears; habeas corpus discharge clearly granted.

enrichment.short_title: Extradition refused for in absentia drug sentence
key_facts: Raffaele Sadutto, an Italian national, was convicted in absentia in 1996 of a serious drug conspiracy and sentenced to eight years plus a revoked suspended sentence.
He had co-operated with Italian investigators against dangerous associates and left Italy fearing for his life when promised protection was not provided.
The sentencing court reduced his sentence for co-operation but less than it would have done had he attended, apparently unaware why he had fled.
Italy sought his extradition from England and he had no right of appeal against the sentence if returned.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Habeas corpus application resisting extradition under sections 6(2) and 11(3) Extradition Act 1989.
enrichment.outcome: Application allowed; extradition would be unjust and the applicant was discharged on unconditional bail pending any further steps.
enrichment.ratio: Where a fugitive was convicted in absentia after leaving the requesting state because co-operation put his life at risk and there is no right of appeal on sentence, return would be unjust even though guilt is accepted and the offence is serious.
legal_issues: Whether conviction in absentia made return contrary to the interests of justice under section 6(2)
Whether passage of time and special circumstances made return oppressive under section 11(3)
Relevance of absence of any right of appeal on sentence
Application of European fair-trial principles where guilt is not in issue
